title: Formulae and calculations (part 2)
learningObjective: Understand how to carry out calculations involving amount of substance, volume and concentration (in mol/dm³) of solution; Understand how to carry out calculations involving gas volumes and the molar volume of a gas (24 dm³ and 24 000 cm³ at room temperature and pressure (rtp))

sections.title: Formulae and calculations (part 2) — the chapter map
sections.markdown:
Part 2 of the formulae-and-calculations chapter extends the mole toolkit you
built in Chapter 5 from **masses** to **gases and solutions**. This
material stands squarely on part 1: everything here is the same
"calculate the moles, use the equation, convert to what's asked" three-stage
method, applied to two new ways of quoting an amount. By the end you will
learn to calculate what volume of gas a reaction produces, and how to work
with solution concentrations quoted in mol/dm³.

The two objectives of record for this lesson are both **Chemistry-only**
specification statements — they are assessed in **Paper 2 only** and are not
shared with Science Double Award:

- calculations involving amount of substance, volume and **concentration (in
  mol/dm³)** of solution (spec 1.34C);
- calculations involving **gas volumes and the molar volume of a gas**
  (24 dm³ and 24 000 cm³ at room temperature and pressure, rtp) (spec 1.35C).

The chapter falls into two clean halves: gas volumes first (Avogadro's law
and the molar volume), then solutions (concentration units, the four worked
examples, and titration calculations). Master both halves and every
gas-and-solution calculation on the course becomes routine.

:::prior-knowledge
You need the part-1 toolkit before starting — the chapter is built on it. Concretely, from Chapter 5 (u1:c05): the mole as the unit for amount of
substance (spec 1.27); moles from mass via mass ÷ mass of 1 mol (spec 1.28);
calculating Mᵣ from Aᵣ values (spec 1.26); the big-numbers-in-front-of-formulae
mole ratios from a balanced equation; and the three-stage method for reacting-mass
problems (spec 1.29). If any of those feel shaky, revisit the relevant sections
of Lesson u1:c05 before going further — every calculation here leans on them.
:::

:::exam-hint
Both of this chapter's spec points carry the **C suffix** (1.34C, 1.35C), which
in Edexcel IGCSE Chemistry means: examined in **Paper 2 (2C) only**, and never
in Science Double Award. Practically: gas-volume and concentration calculations
are Paper-2 bankable marks — the standard titration calculation in particular
appears nearly every series, and it is the same three-stage method every time.
:::

:::misconception
"Part 2 is a new topic, so it needs new methods." It doesn't — it is the same
mole ladder with two new rungs. Mass, gas volume and concentration are three
different currencies for "amount of substance"; the exchange rates are Mᵣ (for
mass), the molar volume 24 dm³ (for gases at rtp) and 1 dm³ of solution (for
concentration). Learners who treat gases and solutions as separate topics
memorise twice; learners who see them as conversions solve unfamiliar problems.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C and 1.35C items — the two-objective map, the
Paper-2-only route badge, and the three-stage method carried over from part
1.
:::

sections.title: Calculations involving gas volumes
sections.markdown:
The gas-volume half of the chapter opens with one of the most striking
ideas in the course: picture three identical flasks holding **different
gases** at the same temperature and pressure — all three contain **equal
numbers of molecules**. Not similar numbers: equal. The identity of the gas
and the size of its molecules simply do not matter.

That single figure is the whole foundation for this half-chapter. If equal
volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, then volumes of gases tell you
directly about **numbers of molecules** — and since moles are just counted
molecules (the Avogadro constant of them per mole), volumes of gases tell you
about **moles** with no Mᵣ and no weighing step at all. The next section
names this statement properly (Avogadro's law) and starts using it on real
equations.

:::exam-hint
When a question gives you volumes of gases and a balanced equation, the
volumes are already "in moles" at the same ratio — do **not** convert them to
masses first. The next section's methane example walks the full reasoning: 100 cm³ of methane needs exactly 200 cm³ of oxygen and yields
exactly 100 cm³ of carbon dioxide, because the big numbers say 1 : 2 : 1.
:::

:::misconception
"Flaskfuls of chlorine must contain more molecules than flaskfuls of hydrogen
— chlorine molecules are bigger and heavier." Size and mass are properties of
each molecule, not of the space between molecules. In a gas the molecules
occupy a negligible fraction of the container; the volume is almost entirely
empty space, and at the same temperature and pressure every gas spaces its
molecules identically. Equal volumes → equal molecule counts, every time.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.35C items — equal volumes at the same temperature
and pressure containing equal numbers of molecules, and reading reacting
volumes straight from a balanced equation.
:::

sections.title: Avogadro's law
sections.markdown:
The law fits in one line, and the line is worth memorising verbatim:
**[[avogadros-law]]** — equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and
pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. So 100 cm³ of hydrogen holds
exactly as many molecules as 100 cm³ of Cl₂ or any other gas under the same
conditions, irrespective of the size of the molecules. One refinement: for
helium and the other noble gases, say "atoms"
rather than "molecules", because they exist as single atoms.

The law becomes a calculating tool the moment you apply it to a balanced
equation. Methane burns:

CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)

The big numbers say 1 methane molecule reacts with 2 oxygen molecules to make
1 carbon dioxide molecule (and 2 water molecules — which, as steam, would
also count as a gas volume; as written here water is the liquid). So **gas
volumes react and form in the same ratio as the big numbers**: react 100 cm³
of methane and you need exactly 200 cm³ of oxygen, and exactly 100 cm³ of
carbon dioxide gas forms. No moles arithmetic needed at this stage — the
volume ratio *is* the mole ratio.

Two flags: the vocabulary and the single most important consequence. The cubic decimetre is the preferred unit (not the litre) when
you mean 1000 cm³. And from the law it follows that **1 mole of any gas
occupies 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³) at rtp** — [[rtp]] meaning room temperature and
pressure, usually taken as 20–25 °C and 1 atmosphere. That consequence is the
molar volume, and the next-but-one section turns it into a calculating tool.

:::key-point
Compressed: for helium and the other
noble gases we say **atoms** instead of molecules; the **cubic decimetre**
(dm³) is the preferred unit for 1000 cm³ — not the litre; and the most
important consequence of Avogadro's law is that **1 mole of any gas occupies
24 dm³ (24 000 cm³) at rtp**.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State the ratio in which the gases react" — read it straight off the big
numbers and quote the volumes in the same ratio, as in the methane example: 100 cm³ of CH₄ needs 200 cm³ of O₂ and forms 100 cm³ of CO₂. Always
name the condition — the ratio holds *at the same temperature and pressure* —
and count only the substances that are actually gases in that equation (the
state symbols tell you which: here H₂O is (l), so it contributes no gas
volume).
:::

:::misconception
"100 cm³ of methane plus 200 cm³ of oxygen must give 300 cm³ of products."
Mass is conserved, but **gas volume is not** — volume depends on how many
molecules of *gas* you end up with, not on total mass. In the methane
reaction the oxygen's volume "disappears" because the water product is
liquid: only 100 cm³ of CO₂(g) remains. Count gas-phase molecules from the
equation; never add volumes like masses.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.35C items — stating Avogadro's law, predicting
reacting/formed gas volumes from big numbers at the same temperature and
pressure, and the 24 dm³ per mole consequence.
:::

sections.title: Units of volume — cm³ and dm³
sections.markdown:
Volumes of gases *and* of solutions are measured in cubic centimetres (cm³)
or cubic decimetres (dm³) — you may also meet the litre, but the last
section already told you the house preference: **1 litre =
1 dm³ = 1000 cm³**, and you should quote cubic decimetres rather than litres.
Everything in this chapter runs on that one conversion, so it is worth being
automatic about it.

Visualise the conversion as a ladder. Because
1 dm³ is equivalent to 1000 cm³, converting **dm³ to cm³ means going from 1
to 1000, so you multiply by 1000**; converting **cm³ to dm³ means going from
1000 down to 1, so you divide by 1000**. The most important thing you
need to be able to do here is exactly this conversion — the molar
volume comes in two sizes (24 dm³ and 24 000 cm³) and the concentration unit
is built on the dm³, so every calculation in this chapter will ask you to
pick the right one.

:::key-point
1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 litre. To convert dm³ → cm³, multiply by 1000; to
convert cm³ → dm³, divide by 1000.
:::

:::exam-hint
The lost-mark scan in every gas-volume or concentration answer: **which unit
is my volume in, and which unit does my constant want?** Molar volume 24 dm³
pairs with volumes in dm³; 24 000 cm³ pairs with volumes in cm³. Mixing them
throws answers out by a factor of 1000 — look carefully: is the volume
given in cm³ or dm³? That error is the most common one in the paper.
:::

:::misconception
"dm³ means cubic metres." It doesn't — the *d* stands for **deci-**, a tenth:
a decimetre is one tenth of a metre, so a cubic decimetre is (0.1 m)³ = one
thousandth of a cubic metre. The cubic metre (m³) is 1000 dm³ — a thousand
times bigger again. Confusing dm³ with m³ is a factor-of-1000 error in the
opposite direction from the cm³ slip.
:::

:::maths-skills
The conversion is a unit-prefix ladder, the same skill as mm → cm → m in
physics: each step of 10³. Write the ladder once (cm³ —×1000→ dm³ —×1000→ m³)
and read off the direction for any problem. Exam-style: convert 350 cm³ to
dm³ (350 ÷ 1000 = 0.350 dm³); convert 2.4 dm³ to cm³ (2.4 × 1000 = 2400 cm³).
Quote the unit in the answer — an unlabelled number is a lost mark in every
calculation question of this chapter.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C and 1.35C items — the cm³/dm³ conversions
that underpin molar-volume and concentration calculations.
:::

sections.title: The molar volume — one mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³
sections.markdown:
Avogadro's law has one consequence that is the most important in the whole
chapter: since 1 mole of any gas contains the same number of molecules
as 1 mole of any other gas, it must occupy **the same volume**. At room
temperature and pressure ([[rtp]] — usually 20–25 °C and 1 atmosphere) that
volume is approximately **24 dm³, or 24 000 cm³**. This is the
**[[molar-volume]]**. It belongs to the conditions, not to the gas: 1 mole of
hydrogen, 1 mole of chlorine, 1 mole of carbon dioxide — 24 dm³ each at rtp.
(Extension: strictly the molar volume has units of dm³/mol — a unit you
are unlikely to meet at International GCSE.)

Two triangles convert between volume and moles the same way the Chapter-5
mass triangle does:

- **volume = number of moles × molar volume**
- **number of moles = volume of gas ÷ molar volume**

Worked straight through: the volume of 0.20 mol of CO₂ at rtp is
0.20 × 24 = **4.8 dm³** (using 24 because the answer is wanted in dm³). Going
the other way, 0.01 g of hydrogen (Aᵣ: H = 1) is 0.01 ÷ 2 = 0.005 mol, which
occupies 0.005 × 24 000 = **120 cm³** — using 24 000 because the question
asks for cm³. And 120 cm³ of carbon dioxide is 120 ÷ 24 000 = **0.005 mol**.
Same triangle every time; the only decision is which size of the molar
volume to substitute.

Now run the full three-stage method — *calculate the moles of
what you can, use the equation to deduce the moles of what you want, convert
to the quantity asked* — on a gas-volume version of the Chapter-5 reacting-mass
problem: **what volume of CO₂ forms when excess dilute hydrochloric acid is
added to 1.00 g of calcium carbonate?** (Aᵣ: C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40; molar
volume = 24 dm³ at rtp.) The equation is
CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l). The acid is in
**[[excess]]** — more than enough to react with all the calcium carbonate —
so the CaCO₃ sets the yield. Mᵣ of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + (3 × 16) = 100, so
1.00 g is 1.00 ÷ 100 = 0.0100 mol. The equation says 1 mol CaCO₃ produces
1 mol CO₂, so 0.0100 mol of CO₂ forms; converting with the molar volume in
dm³ gives 0.0100 × 24 = **0.24 dm³**. The closing warning is the
exam-hint below.

:::key-point
1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ (24 000 cm³) at rtp — the same for every
gas. The unit law: volume given in cm³ → use 24 000 cm³; volume given in
dm³ → use 24 dm³.
:::

:::exam-hint
"It is really important to include the units here because the examiner will
not know whether you mean cm³ or dm³ unless you write it down" — the
whole point for the 0.0100 × 24 = 0.24 dm³ answer. Quote the unit with
every intermediate and final volume, and match the constant to the unit
before you multiply, not after.
:::

:::misconception
"24 dm³ is a property of the gas — hydrogen occupies a different molar volume
from chlorine." At the same temperature and pressure, no: the molar volume is
fixed by Avogadro's law, not by the gas's identity. What *does* change with
conditions is the value itself — 24 dm³ is an **rtp** number; at STP (0 °C,
1 atm) the molar volume is different. Read the conditions in the question and
use the value the question pins (every 4CH1 question at rtp gives or implies
24 dm³ / 24 000 cm³).
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.35C items — moles ↔ volume conversions via 24 dm³
/ 24 000 cm³, and three-stage gas-volume problems with an excess reagent.
:::

sections.title: Worked problem — making hydrogen from aluminium
sections.markdown:
The chapter's first full gas-volume problem runs the three stages in the
direction that feels backwards: from a **volume** of gas wanted to a **mass**
of solid needed. Aluminium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid:

2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) → 2AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂(g)

*What mass of aluminium would you need to add to an [[excess]] of dilute
hydrochloric acid so that you produced 100 cm³ of hydrogen at room
temperature and pressure? (Aᵣ of Al = 27; molar volume = 24 000 cm³ at rtp.)*

**Stage 1 — moles of what we can.** We can only calculate the moles of the
hydrogen; the mass of aluminium is the unknown. The volume is in cm³, so use
the molar volume as 24 000 cm³: number of moles of H₂ = 100 ÷ 24 000 =
**0.00417 mol**, written in standard form as 4.17 × 10⁻³ mol.

**Stage 2 — equation ratio.** The big numbers say 3 mol of H₂ are produced
from 2 mol of Al. So the moles of Al are **two-thirds** of the moles of H₂:
0.00417 × 2/3 = **0.00278 mol** of aluminium.

**Stage 3 — convert to the asked quantity.** mass = number of moles × mass of
1 mol = 0.00278 × 27 = **0.075 g of Al**.

Two boxes below earn their place as examiner advice, and they target the
two classic slips: mangling the 3-to-2 ratio, and then double-counting the 2 in
the final mass step.

:::exam-hint
The ratio step: to go from 3 (H₂) to 2 (Al), divide the 3
by 3 to get 1 and multiply by 2 to get 2 — in other words, multiply the moles
of H₂ by **2/3**. The same divide-then-multiply routine works for any ratio
the equation hands you, forwards or backwards.
:::

:::misconception
"Moles of Al = 0.00417 × 54, because the equation has 2Al and Aᵣ of Al is 27."
That double-counts the 2 — the correction: **multiply by 27, not 54**. The 2 in front of the Al was already used in the ratio step
(2 mol Al per 3 mol H₂). The mass of 0.00278 mol of Al is fixed at 0.00278 ×
27: the mass of a given number of moles cannot depend on what the aluminium
is reacting with.
:::

:::cross-curricular
Maths — standard form and ratios. The intermediate answer 0.00417 mol is
written in standard form, 4.17 × 10⁻³ mol: small mole counts in gas
problems
regularly demand confident standard form, and the "divide by 3, multiply by
2" ratio move is the same proportion skill as map scales and recipe
scaling. Both are Paper-2 quantitative skills shared with the maths
qualification.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.35C items — mass-to-volume and volume-to-mass
problems through an equation ratio at rtp.
:::

sections.title: Working with solution concentrations
sections.markdown:
The solutions half of the chapter begins with the two concentration units.
Concentrations can be measured in **g/dm³** or in **mol/dm³** — also written g dm⁻³ and
mol dm⁻³, and read as "grams per cubic decimetre" and "moles per cubic
decimetre". Both units ride on the **[[cubic-decimetre]]** from the last
unit section: remember that 1 dm³ is the same as 1 litre. (You may also meet
the symbol **[[molarity]]** — a concentration quoted as "2 M" means
2 mol/dm³.)

The core skill is converting **between g/dm³ and mol/dm³**, and the point
is reassuring: *this is no different from converting moles into
grams and vice versa* — multiply or divide by the Mᵣ. It makes no difference
that the substance is dissolved in 1 dm³ of solution; the arithmetic is the
Chapter-5 mass↔moles ladder wearing a per-dm³ hat.

The worked case: sea water with a sodium chloride concentration of
**35.1 g/dm³** — find the concentration in mol/dm³ (Aᵣ: Na = 23, Cl = 35.5).
1 mol of NaCl has a mass of 58.5 g. Every dm³ of solution holds 35.1 g, so
the moles in every dm³ are 35.1 ÷ 58.5 = **0.600 mol**. The concentration is
therefore **0.600 mol/dm³** — sea water holds about 0.6 moles of NaCl per
cubic decimetre.

:::key-point
Two concentration units, one bridge: **g/dm³ → mol/dm³ is ÷ Mᵣ; mol/dm³ →
g/dm³ is × Mᵣ** (per dm³ of solution, exactly as mass ↔ moles in Chapter 5).
:::

:::exam-hint
Quote concentration answers **with the unit the question asked for** — a bare
"0.600" scores nothing when the question said mol/dm³. And when a question
hands you a concentration in one unit and the equation mole-ratio arithmetic
needs moles, convert to mol/dm³ first: mole ratios only ever apply to
moles, never to grams.
:::

:::misconception
"Concentration in g/dm³ tells you how many moles you have." Not until you
divide by Mᵣ — 35.1 g/dm³ of NaCl and 35.1 g/dm³ of NaHCO₃ are different
mole counts, because the formula units have different masses. The g/dm³
number is a mass in every dm³; only ÷ Mᵣ turns it into an amount of
substance.
:::

:::maths-skills
The two-unit ladder is a proportional-reasoning chain: g/dm³ —(÷ Mᵣ)→
mol/dm³, and dm³ of solution —(× concentration)→ moles. Exam-style with those
numbers: 35.1 g/dm³ of NaCl (Mᵣ 58.5) = 0.600 mol/dm³; then 2.0 dm³
of that sea water holds 2.0 × 0.600 = 1.2 mol of NaCl. Three conversions,
one skill: keep the units attached to every number and let them cancel like
fractions.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — the two concentration units, the Mᵣ
bridge between them, and concentration → moles for a stated volume.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 1 — concentration from mol/dm³ to g/dm³
sections.markdown:
Example 1 runs the × Mᵣ direction of the bridge. *What is the
concentration of a 0.050 mol/dm³ solution of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, in
g/dm³? (Aᵣ: C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23.)*

Reason per dm³ of solution — the cleanest way to see the units do the
work:

1. 1 dm³ of solution contains **0.050 mol** of Na₂CO₃.
2. Mᵣ of Na₂CO₃ = (2 × 23) + 12 + (3 × 16) = **106**, so 1 mol weighs 106 g.
3. 0.050 mol weighs 0.050 × 106 = **5.3 g**.
4. 1 dm³ of solution contains 5.3 g — so the concentration is **5.3 g/dm³**.

Notice the structure: the question was per-dm³ in, per-dm³ out, and the only
arithmetic was the moles → grams conversion you have used since Chapter 5.
Every "convert a mol/dm³ concentration into g/dm³" question in the paper is
this four-line shape with different numbers.

:::exam-hint
Mark-scheme-friendly layout: write the Mᵣ line explicitly ((2 × 23) + 12 +
(3 × 16) = 106) — the Mᵣ itself usually carries a mark — then the multiply
line with units. The × Mᵣ direction check: mol/dm³ → g/dm³ must make the
number **bigger** (you are counting formula-unit masses); if your g/dm³
answer comes out smaller than your mol/dm³ number, you divided instead.
:::

:::misconception
"0.050 mol/dm³ is a small number, so 0.050 g/dm³ is the answer." The two
units are not interchangeable decimals — the Mᵣ bridges them and it is never
1. Here 0.050 mol/dm³ becomes 5.3 g/dm³, a hundredfold bigger, because each
formula unit has a mass of 106 g. Always × or ÷ by the Mᵣ; never equate the
two numbers.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — mol/dm³ → g/dm³ conversions with an
explicit Mᵣ step.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 2 — concentration in mol/dm³ from grams
sections.markdown:
Example 2 runs the ÷ Mᵣ direction, with one extra twist: the solution volume
is not 1 dm³. *What is the concentration in mol/dm³ of a solution containing
2.1 g of sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, in 250 cm³ of solution? (Aᵣ:
H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, Na = 23.)*

1. Mᵣ of NaHCO₃ = 23 + 1 + 12 + (3 × 16) = **84**, so 1 mol has a mass of 84 g.
2. 2.1 g is 2.1 ÷ 84 = **0.025 mol**.
3. That 0.025 mol sits in 250 cm³ — but concentration wants *per 1000 cm³*.
   There are four lots of 250 cm³ in 1000 cm³, so scale up: 4 × 0.025 =
   **0.10 mol** in 1 dm³.
4. The concentration is **0.10 mol/dm³**.

The solution triangle is the shortcut for steps 3 and 4 — the same
triangle the next section turns into the single most-used equation of the
topic.

That hint is aimed at the questions you will actually meet:
*"when doing calculations involving solutions you will most often be asked to
calculate a number of moles given the volume of the solution and its
concentration"*, via:

**number of moles = volume of solution (dm³) × concentration (mol/dm³)**

— and because concentrations come in mol/dm³ while volumes usually come in
cm³, you **usually have to convert the volume to dm³ by dividing by 1000**
first. The HINT's reassurance about unfamiliar formulae is worth keeping too:
meet an equation containing, say, CH₃COOH (ethanoic acid) in a later
question, and the concentration arithmetic does not care — it only needs the
volume, the concentration and the big numbers.

:::exam-hint
The scaling shortcut generalises: whatever the volume, dividing by it and
multiplying by 1000 is the same as "per dm³". 250 cm³ → ×4; 200 cm³ → ×5;
50 cm³ → ×20. But in the exam the safest habit is the triangle's algebra:
moles = (volume ÷ 1000) × concentration — write the ÷1000 line visibly,
because that is the mark the marker looks for.
:::

:::misconception
"0.025 mol in 250 cm³ means a concentration of 0.025 mol/dm³." That ignores
the per-dm³ scale-up: the concentration must state what is in **1000 cm³**.
The tell is the unit sanity check — a solution made from 2.1 g in a quarter
of a dm³ reading "0.025 mol/dm³" would hold just 0.025 mol in a full dm³,
i.e. less in more, which contradicts dissolving the same solid. Scale to the
dm³ before quoting the unit.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — grams → mol/dm³ with a non-dm³
solution volume, and the moles = volume × concentration law.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 3 — moles from volume and concentration
sections.markdown:
Example 3 is that most-used equation in action — the single most reusable
line of the solutions half. *Calculate the number of moles of NaOH in 50 cm³ of
0.10 mol/dm³ solution.*

1. Convert the volume: 50 ÷ 1000 = **0.050 dm³**.
2. Apply the equation: number of moles = volume of solution (dm³) ×
   concentration (mol/dm³).
3. Number of moles = 0.050 × 0.10 = **0.0050 mol**.

That three-line shape — ÷1000, then × concentration — is the standard opener
of every solution calculation from here to the end of the course: titrations
(s12–s14), the limescale problem (s11), and later units' acid-base work all
start by converting "V cm³ of c mol/dm³" into a mole count this way. Note
the trailing zeros (0.050, 0.0050): they are significant figures, and
preserving them keeps the working honest about precision.

:::exam-hint
The two-step dance appears in every mark scheme as two separate marks:
**M1** for converting the volume (÷1000) or for the correct substitution into
moles = V × c, and **A1** for the evaluated mole count. Writing 50/1000 ×
0.10 in one visible line earns the first mark even if the arithmetic later
slips — which is why the layout converts first, then multiplies, as
separate displayed steps.
:::

:::misconception
"50 cm³ of 0.10 mol/dm³ contains 5 mol — 50 × 0.10." The volume must be in
dm³, and 50 cm³ is 0.050 dm³, not 50 dm³. The wrong answer is a thousandfold
too big. Quick sense-check that catches this every time: 1 dm³ of 0.10
mol/dm³ holds 0.10 mol, so 50 cm³ — a twentieth of a dm³ — must hold a
twentieth of that, 0.0050 mol.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — moles from volume × concentration
with a cm³ → dm³ conversion.
:::

sections.title: Calculations with equations involving solutions
sections.markdown:
Now the two halves of the chapter merge: solution arithmetic feeding the
three-stage method through a balanced equation. The context is domestic
chemistry — limescale (calcium carbonate) removed from kettles by a
dilute acid, such as the ethanoic acid in vinegar:

CaCO₃(s) + 2CH₃COOH(aq) → (CH₃COO)₂Ca(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

*What mass of calcium carbonate can be removed by 50 cm³ of a solution of
ethanoic acid that has a concentration of 2 mol/dm³? (Aᵣ: C = 12, O = 16,
Ca = 40.)*

**Stage 1 — moles of what we can.** We know the volume and concentration of
the acid: convert the volume to dm³ by dividing by 1000, then
number of moles of ethanoic acid = (50 ÷ 1000) × 2 = **0.1 mol**.

**Stage 2 — equation ratio.** The equation has a **2** in front of the
CH₃COOH but no number (meaning 1) in front of the CaCO₃, so 2 mol of acid
react with 1 mol of CaCO₃ — the moles of CaCO₃ are **half** the moles of
acid: 0.1 ÷ 2 = **0.05 mol** of CaCO₃.

**Stage 3 — convert to the asked quantity.** Mᵣ of CaCO₃ = 100, so
mass = 0.05 × 100 = **5 g** of calcium carbonate removed.

This is the same skeleton as the hydrogen problem (s06) and the CaCO₃
problem (s05) — only the stage-1 conversion changes, from molar volume to
volume × concentration. "Again, we will use our three stages" is
deliberate: by now the method, not the chemistry, is the transferable skill.

:::exam-hint
The ratio extraction deserves its own written line: "2 mol CH₃COOH : 1 mol
CaCO₃, so moles CaCO₃ = moles acid ÷ 2". Mark schemes award the ratio line
even when the arithmetic fails, and the half-it habit (÷2 when your substance
has the bigger coefficient) is safer than cross-multiplying in your head.
State the equation's big numbers before using them.
:::

:::misconception
"The acid's coefficient 2 means the acid is twice as concentrated, so use
2 mol/dm³ differently." No — the 2 is already spent the moment the
concentration is multiplied in: 0.050 dm³ × 2 mol/dm³ is 0.1 mol **of acid**,
full stop. The coefficient re-enters only in stage 2 as the reacting ratio
between the substances. Never fold equation coefficients into the
concentration; keep stage 1 (how many moles of *this* solution) and stage 2
(how the *substances* relate) cleanly apart.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — three-stage problems where a
solution's volume × concentration opens the chain.
:::

sections.title: Calculations from titrations
sections.markdown:
Everything so far has been calculation technique; the **[[titration]]** is
the experiment that feeds it. A titration finds out *how much of one solution
reacts with a certain volume of another solution of known concentration*.
The apparatus: a solution of alkali is measured into a conical flask with a **[[pipette]]** (one accurate, fixed volume), and the acid is
run in from a **[[burette]]** (a variable, read-off volume), swirling the
flask constantly. Towards the end the acid goes in a drop at a time until
the indicator just changes colour — the **[[endpoint]]**. Acid–alkali titration
technique itself is developed in Chapters 16 and 17; here it is the *numbers*
that matter.

The logic of the calculation: if you know the concentration of either the
acid or the alkali, the titration hands you the other piece of the pair — a
volume of solution of known concentration reacting exactly with a volume of
the unknown. That is precisely one volume × concentration term and one
unknown concentration: the standard three stages with the burette readings
as stage-1 data.

Two hints on titration practice are examiner-neutral and worth pinning
now, before the standard calculation uses them.

:::exam-hint
The two hints, in substance: (1) *the acid and alkali can be
added the other way round, with the alkali in the burette* — the
concentration calculation does not care which reagent sat where, only which
volumes reacted; (2) *remember to divide the volume by 1000 to convert to
dm³* — burette and pipette readings come in cm³, and every concentration in
this family is per dm³.
:::

:::misconception
"The endpoint tells you the acid and alkali are equal." The endpoint tells
you the *reaction is just complete* — the reacting amounts are in the
**equation's mole ratio**, which is 1 : 1 for NaOH + HCl but 2 : 1 for
2NaOH + H₂SO₄. Equal volumes of the two solutions are a coincidence of
concentrations, not a law; the mole ratio, never the volume equality, drives
stage 2.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — titration apparatus roles and the
volume-data logic of the titration calculation.
:::

sections.title: The standard titration calculation
sections.markdown:
Here is the shape of *a standard titration problem* — learn this
layout and nearly every titration question in the paper is a re-skin:

*25.00 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide solution required 23.50 cm³ of
dilute hydrochloric acid for neutralisation. Calculate the concentration of
the hydrochloric acid.*

NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)

**Stage 1 — moles of what we can.** We know both the volume and the
concentration of the sodium hydroxide: number of moles of NaOH =
(25.00 ÷ 1000) × 0.100 = **0.00250 mol**.

**Stage 2 — equation ratio.** The equation says 1 mol of NaOH reacts with
1 mol of HCl, so 0.00250 mol of NaOH reacts with **0.00250 mol of HCl**.

**Stage 3 — convert to the asked quantity.** That 0.00250 mol of HCl is what
was in the 23.50 cm³ the titration measured out — so the acid's
concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³ = 0.00250 ÷ (23.50 ÷ 1000) =
**0.106 mol/dm³**.

The closing line for this example is the checkpoint: *we have the volume
and number of moles of HCl and can work out the concentration*. Stage
3 in a titration is always the concentration rearrangement — moles ÷ (volume
÷ 1000) — rather than a mass conversion, which is the only structural
difference from s11's limescale problem.

:::exam-hint
The titration mark scheme, in this order every time: **M1** moles of the
known solution (volume ÷ 1000 × concentration); **M1** the equation ratio
quoted and applied; **M1** concentration = moles ÷ volume with the *other*
volume converted to dm³; **A1** the value with mol/dm³. Carry at least
3 significant figures through the intermediate steps (0.00250, not 0.003) —
rounding before the last line is the classic titration mark leak. Note the
data style too: 25.00 cm³ and 23.50 cm³ — burette readings to 2 decimal
places, exactly what Chapter 16's technique will demand.
:::

:::misconception
"The concentration of the acid is 0.00250 ÷ 25.00..." — mixing up *which*
volume pairs with *which* moles. The 0.00250 mol of HCl sits in the acid's
23.50 cm³, not in the alkali's 25.00 cm³; the alkali's data was already used
in stage 1. Anchor each intermediate to its substance ("0.00250 mol **of
HCl** in **23.50 cm³ of acid**") and the rearrangement cannot pick the wrong
volume.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — the standard 1 : 1 titration
concentration calculation with cm³ → dm³ conversions.
:::

sections.title: A very slightly harder titration — the 2 : 1 ratio
sections.markdown:
Same apparatus, same stages, one twist: the equation's ratio is not 1 : 1.
*25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration was titrated
with dilute sulfuric acid of concentration 0.050 mol/dm³. 20.0 cm³ of the
acid was required to neutralise the alkali. Find the concentration of the
sodium hydroxide solution in mol/dm³.*

2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)

**Stage 1 — moles of what we can.** This time everything is known about the
sulfuric acid: moles of H₂SO₄ = (20.0 ÷ 1000) × 0.050 = **0.0010 mol**.

**Stage 2 — the ratio is the whole difficulty.** *The equation proportions
aren't 1 : 1 this time — that's what makes the
calculation slightly different from the last one.* The equation shows 1 mol
of sulfuric acid reacts with **2 mol** of sodium hydroxide, so moles of NaOH
= 2 × 0.0010 = **0.0020 mol**.

**Stage 3 — concentration.** That 0.0020 mol must have been in the 25.0 cm³
(25.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 dm³) of sodium hydroxide: concentration =
0.0020 ÷ 0.025 = **0.080 mol/dm³**.

The reverse family exists too — *instead of calculating a concentration
from titration results, you may be asked to calculate what volume of a
solution is needed to neutralise something else* — and Example 4 in the
next section runs that shape.

:::exam-hint
When the ratio is 2 : 1, say which way it doubles *in words* before
multiplying: "1 mol acid reacts with 2 mol alkali, so moles NaOH = 2 × moles
H₂SO₄". Mark schemes routinely place the ratio mark before the arithmetic —
and note the trap direction: here the *unknown* (NaOH) gets the 2, so the
answer 0.080 mol/dm³ is **bigger** than the acid's 0.050 mol/dm³. A quick
proportion sanity check (more concentrated alkali for the same neutralising
power in less volume... here slightly more volume, so mildly more
concentrated) catches inverted ratios.
:::

:::misconception
"Balance the equation to make the ratio 1 : 1, then divide evenly." You
cannot re-arrange the chemistry to suit the arithmetic — 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ is
the reaction; the 2 : 1 mole ratio is a fact of the substances, not a
nuisance. Doubling the NaOH data or halving the acid data to "simplify" the
ratio fabricates a different experiment. Apply the ratio; don't remove it.
:::

:::quick-check

Question-bank join: spec 1.34C items — titration calculations with a 2 : 1
(or 1 : 2) equation ratio in either direction.
:::

sections.title: Worked example 4 — reversing the calculation, and the chapter close
sections.markdown:
The chapter's last worked example runs the stages backwards: instead of a
concentration, the unknown is a **volume** of solution. *Calculate the volume
of 0.100 mol/dm³ sodium hydrogencarbonate (NaHCO₃) solution needed to
neutralise 20.0 cm³ of 0.125 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid (HCl).*

NaHCO₃(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

**Stage 1.** Only the acid is fully known: moles of HCl = (20.0 ÷ 1000) ×
0.125 = **0.00250 mol** — *we do not have enough information to calculate the
number of moles of anything else, so must start here*.

**Stage 2.** The equation is 1 : 1, so the same **0.00250 mol** of NaHCO₃ is
needed.

**Stage 3 — volume instead of mass or concentration.** Rearrange the
concentration equation: volume = moles ÷ concentration = 0.00250 ÷ 0.100 =
**0.0250 dm³** (the volume comes out in dm³ because the concentration is in
mol/dm³), then × 1000 for the answer the question wants: **25.0 cm³** of
sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.

The chapter closes with a self-check of everything it built — gas volumes
at rtp (including potassium nitrate and chlorine preparation problems),
g/dm³ ↔ mol/dm³ conversions, mass-from-concentration problems, and a full
titration set. This lesson's practice is wired to the question bank below.

:::summary
In one page: **gases** — Avogadro's law says equal volumes (same temperature
and pressure) hold equal molecules, so 1 mol of *any* gas occupies 24 dm³
(24 000 cm³) at rtp; moles = volume ÷ molar volume (matching cm³ to 24 000
and dm³ to 24), and gas volumes react in the equation's big-number ratio.
**Solutions** — concentration is per dm³: g/dm³ ÷ Mᵣ = mol/dm³ (and × Mᵣ
back); moles = volume (÷1000) × concentration. **Everywhere** — the
three-stage method: moles of what you can, equation ratio, convert to what
is asked. Titration = the experiment that measures the reacting volumes.
:::

:::can-you
- State Avogadro's law, and say why 1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm³ at rtp? (1.35C)
- Convert 250 cm³ to dm³, and 2.4 dm³ to cm³, without hesitation? (1.35C)
- Calculate the volume of a stated number of moles (or mass) of gas at rtp — like the 0.20 mol CO₂ and 0.01 g H₂ examples? (1.35C)
- Work a full gas-volume problem through an equation ratio, like the aluminium/hydrogen problem? (1.35C)
- Convert a concentration between g/dm³ and mol/dm³ using Mᵣ, both directions? (1.34C)
- Calculate moles from a volume and concentration — with the ÷1000 — like Example 3? (1.34C)
- Run the standard titration calculation, including a 2 : 1 ratio, and a reversed volume question like Example 4? (1.34C)
:::

:::exam-hint
The Paper-2 pattern across this chapter: one gas-volume calculation
(molar volume at rtp, usually via an equation) and one solution
concentration calculation (usually a titration) are near-permanent fixtures.
Both are three-stage questions — full marks come from the *layout*, not
luck: convert first (÷1000 or ÷ molar volume), quote the ratio from the
equation, rearrange last, units on every line.
:::

:::misconception
"Example 4 needs a new method because the answer is a volume of *solution*."
It is the same rearrangement as the molar-volume triangle, pointed at the
solution triangle: moles ÷ concentration = volume in dm³. The only genuinely
new content in the whole chapter was two conversion constants — the molar
volume and the mol/dm³ definition — and both now sit inside the same
three-stage method you brought from part 1.
:::
